title: What is known about 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_1RC---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_1RC---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. It belongs to a family of four holdouts that share their first four states, and works as two binary counters, one counting down in the blocks left of the head and one counting up in the gaps right of it. This page lists what is established, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean now proves the counter itself: read the tape as two binary numbers, E in the odd blocks left of the head and N in the gaps right of it, and every countdown of E, for every size of E and N, runs as the counter says (run3, run5). Lean also proves that the blank-tape run enters this counter after 160 steps and runs its first countdown. The pass rules (including the halting one) are proved too.

Coq now proves that halting is equivalent to a question about one explicit map, for 1a and 1b at once: the machine halts if and only if the round map of a closed counter model, iterated from (2, 5), reaches a corner X = 2L (halts_iff_corner). The second-overflow cascade is proved too, and it narrows the door to one equation: a corner comes only from rule R5 with the unread rest m of the right counter equal to (2D + 1)·2s − 1, D being how far the left counter is below full (halts_iff_r5_match, also in Lean for the model). Whether the orbit ever meets it is open; in 400,000 rounds (L up to 132 million) it stayed at least 0.47·L bits away.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: The pass rules
claims.text: Six rules on symbolic tapes, for all values of their parameters and any surrounding tape: a pass on an even top block (L 1 A>0 1^(2k+4) 0^(g+2) 1 R), on a block of 2, on an odd block crossing j small gaps, on a block of 3, a gap of length one closing, and pass_odd_halt: an odd pass whose D-run meets a gap one cell too short reaches F reading a 1, the only halting transition. Proofs by rfl steps and crossing lemmas, written by tools/py/bbtools/symtm.py.

claims.title: 1a and 1b agree on F0 followed by 0
claims.text: From L x F>0 0 R both 1RB1LA_..._1RB0RF_0RB--- and 1RB1LA_..._1RB0RF_1RC--- reach L A>x 1 1 R in 3 steps (f00_0, f00_1). The two machines differ only when F reads a 0 followed by a 1.

claims.title: The counter, proved for every size
claims.text: Write E in p bits on the left (from the head outward, a 0 bit is 1 1 and a 1 bit is 1 0, above a floor that starts with a 1) and N in n bits on the right (a 0 bit is 0^3, a 1 bit is 0^2 1, followed by any tape X). In mode 3 (top block 1^3) the machine takes (E, N) to (E − k, N + k) for every k ≤ E with N + k < 2n, in at least 22·k steps (run3); in mode 5 (top block 1^5) it takes (E, N) to (E − k, N + 2k) in at least 48·k steps (run5). Proofs: three pass-pair rules written by tools/py/bbtools/symtm.py, the binary decrement and increment on bit lists, and induction on k.

claims.title: The blank-tape run enters the counter
claims.text: After 160 steps from blank tape the machine is in mode 5 with E = 17 (5 bits) and N = 1 (init_counter), and it then counts E down to 0, reaching N = 35 after at least 816 further steps (first_countdown).

claims.title: A halt needs a corner round (Coq, on busycoq's definitions)
claims.text: halts_needs_corner b : halts (machine b) c0 -> exists j len, iter_n j (cfgL 2 0 5) = Some (cfgL len 0 (2^len)), for both 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_0RB--- (b = false) and 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_1RC---. SOC23Model.v is a closed counter model: a left counter of digits 10/11, a right counter of digits 100/000 and two shifted right counters, with eight raw rules (increments, overflows and five rebuild rules), each proved for every parameter by busycoq's symbolic execution for both tables; a computable step f on configurations with an invariant P, with f_spec: from a P configuration f either gives a configuration the machine reaches and P keeps, or stops, and it stops only at a corner cfgL len 0 (2^len). SOC23_Holdouts.v proves that both machines reach cfgL 2 0 5 from blank tape. Print Assumptions: closed under the global context. Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch (commit 33209bc), 30 seconds for both files.

claims.title: Every corner halts, so halting is equivalent to reaching a corner (Coq)
claims.text: halts_iff_corner bb : halts (machine bb) c0 <-> exists j len, iter_n j (cfgL 2 0 5) = Some (cfgL len 0 (2^len)), for both 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_0RB--- and 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_1RC---. The new half is corner_halts: from a corner cfgL len 0 (2^len), for every len ≥ 1, the machine halts. The path is the same for every len: the overflow of the left counter (LC_Ov) turns the full right counter into a shifted counter that is twice too large, and the left counter is counted all the way down (2len − 1 pairs); the left counter overflows a second time, gains one digit (rule E1), and the right part becomes a counter of len − 1 digits ended by 0011; that counter is counted up through all its values twice, the carry between the two passes turning 0011 into 1011; then a fixed sweep halts (rule Hend). E1 and Hend are tape rules with free parameters, proved for both tables by busycoq's symbolic execution; the rest reuses the counter lemmas of SOC23Model.v. Print Assumptions: closed under the global context. Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch (commit 33209bc), 31 seconds for the three files.

claims.title: A corner can only come from one equation at one rule (Coq)
claims.text: halts_iff_r5_match bb : halts (machine bb) c0 <-> exists j x, iter_n j (cfgL 2 0 5) = Some x /\ r5match x, for both 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_0RB--- and 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_1RC---. After the left counter overflows, the right counter is read as a cascade of second overflows (the place where busycoq's SOC_2_3_v2 template needs its rules ROv2_0 and ROv2_1; here rules R1 to R5 of SOC23Model.v). Call a configuration doomed when its plain countdown ends at a corner (cfgR len k n with k + n + 1 = 2len). doom_step: the only step of the model that makes a doomed configuration out of one that is not doomed is rule R5, a shifted counter cfgS1 with an odd number h = 2a + 1 of digits running out, and only when the unread rest m of the right counter satisfies m + 1 = (2D + 1)·23a+3, where D = 2len − 1 − k is how far the left counter is below full (r5match). The three ends with nothing left to read (R1, R2, R3) never give a corner: the new left counter is an odd number times 2s, minus 1, so the countdown ends one or two short of a power of two. The one exception, cfgS0 len (2^len-1) 0 0 0, is reached by no step (bad0_step). So the second-overflow cascade is proved for every parameter, and what it would take to make a corner is exactly one equation; whether the orbit ever satisfies it is the open question. Print Assumptions: closed under the global context. Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch (commit 33209bc), 2 seconds on top of the other three files.

claims.title: The cascade lemma in Lean
claims.text: lean/Cascade.lean copies the model step f of SOC23Model.v case for case and proves the same lemmas for the model alone: doom_step, bad0_step, and corner_iff_r5, the orbit from cfgL 2 0 5 reaches a corner if and only if it reaches an R5 configuration with m + 1 = (2D + 1)·23a+3. It takes as a hypothesis that every step keeps the invariant P, which Coq proves (f_spec); the link to the machines (halts_iff_corner) is in Coq. Core Lean 4.34, no Mathlib, no sorry.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 137 cells have been visited and 63 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 2·10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: Direct simulation with tools/c/tmrun.c.

claims.title: The counter rule on 4.7 million cycles
claims.text: On the regular shape (head A on 0, 1^5 or 1^3 to its right, then gaps 0^(3q+2) 1) every one of 4,687,473 consecutive cycles of 1a between steps 1,500 and 3·108 takes (E, F) to (E − 1, F + 1) as the two-counter model says, and takes 48 + 4v + 6j steps (v, j read off the top block and the leading gaps). 1a and 1b have the same run here: in their first 109 steps F is entered 6 times, always on a 0 followed by a 0.

claims.title: No halt before 2.53·10<sup>819</sup> steps
claims.text: The round-2 accelerator py/jump2.py (with c/ps.c, in the folder of 1a) simulates directly from pass start to pass start until the tape is a counter configuration of lean/Counter.lean (top block 3 or 5, E and N readable with at least 12 bits), then jumps a whole countdown at once: k cycles with k up to E (or down to the next power of two) and within the room N has before its first defect. Each jump is an instance of run3/run5, so its end tape is proved; only the Python reading of the tape, the exact step count (fitted formula a + 4ν(E) + 6ν(N+1) per pair) and the direct simulation between jumps are unproved. Jumps of at most 108 steps were each re-run by direct simulation and matched token for token. In about 15 minutes on one core it made 107 jumps and reached step 2.53·10819 with no halt (the run was stopped there, not by a failure).

claims.title: Defects stay single
claims.text: In the 6.3 million passes that the round-2 run of 1b simulated directly (between its 107 jumps), the right part never held more than one defect, never more than one 1^2 block, and the fatal precursor (a gap one cell short directly followed by a block of two or more) never occurred.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/fixed
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.036).

claims.title: The phase transition
claims.text: When E reaches 0 the floor block 1^(2s) under it is popped into the top block, the next pass pushes s single 1s, and a new countdown starts with E = 2s − 1 (s one bits; floor 1^2) in the other mode (3 and 5 alternate); N stays on the right, but the cut leaves a gap of irregular size in front of it. Irregular gaps then act in a cascade of short sub-phases: a gap one too long (for 1a/1b; the analogous residue mod 5 for 1c/1d) collapses into a block 1^2, a gap one too short followed by a single 1 is cut down and passes its defect on to the next gap; sometimes the whole of N is pulled to the left and N restarts at 0. The floor grows by 2 whenever E passes a power of two, so it is about twice the bit length of the largest E so far. Seen at every transition of the runs above; not proved, and no closed formula for the new (E, N) as a function of the old one is known.
claims.where: holdouts/1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_0RB---/py/jump2.py (log of the tapes at each counter start)

claims.title: How long a corner takes to halt
claims.text: Started from the corner tape 0^inf 1 (11)^L A>1 1 (000)^L 100 0^inf both machines halt after exactly 2L+5 − 3L − 18 steps, for L = 1, …, 12 (direct simulation). That a corner halts is now proved for every L (corner_halts, above); the step count is the checked part.

claims.title: The model orbit avoids corners for 400,000 rounds
claims.text: The round map of the model (one round from cfgL L 0 X to the next, countdowns jumped at once), iterated from (L, X) = (2, 5) with exact integers for 400,000 rounds: never a corner. L reaches 132,154,476 digits, and after round 4 X − 2L always has at least 0.47·L bits (the closest approach is at round 34). Only rounds 4 and 9 read all of X; round 10 read 53% of it, and from round 35 on no round read more than 22.3% (round 3,305). The GMP port c/model23.c agrees with py/model23.py on (L, X mod 264) at rounds 1 to 3 and 3,000. The first rounds match the real run of 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_0RB---: (2, 5) → (7, 73) → (18, 254409), the last at step 4,071,896.

claims.title: What a corner would take
claims.text: Write the left counter by its deficit D = 2len − 1 − k. A round starts with D = 0; a countdown of n adds n to D, and an overflow that appends s digits sends D to (2D+1)·2s, so the round never needs L itself. The round reads X from its low end and ends either when all of X is read (rules R1, R2, R3 on an empty rest) or at rule R5, which leaves the unread top part m of X. Then X' = 2L' − (2D+1)·2s + m + 1 at R5, and X' = 2L' − (2D+1)·2s (+1 for R1) otherwise. So a corner can only come from R5 with m + 1 = (2D+1)·2s (the R1 case would need X = 1): the part of X a round leaves unread must equal a number computed from the part it read. That number has about 2.5 times as many bits as the part read (a zero run of length h adds about 2h+1 to D and then about 1.5h digits), so a corner needs one round to read about 0.29·L bits of X and the other 0.71·L bits to match exactly (a random match has odds of about 2−0.7L). Only round 10 read that much (53%, right after round 9 had read all of X); from round 35 on no round read more than 22.3%. Derived by hand from f in SOC23Model.v; c/model23.c computes rounds in this form and agrees with py/model23.py. No invariant that excludes the match is known: the low bits of X decide where a round stops, and the top bits are what earlier rounds left, which is what makes the question Collatz-like.

claims.title: How a round reads X, and why sizes do not settle it
claims.text: A round reads X from its low end as runs 0^h 1, and the model only looks at the parity of each h, so the cascade is a reader with four states (S0 or S1, h even or odd): in S0 an even run moves to S1 and an odd run stays in S0; in S1 with h even, a 0 next starts another run in S1 and a 1 next swallows a whole block 1^j 0 and moves to S0 with h = j; in S1 with h odd the round stops (rule R5). All 3,000 first rounds but two (rounds 3 and 8, which read all of X) end at R5. At R5 the equation m + 1 = (2D + 1)·2s first needs the low s bits of m to be 1s and the next one 0; that happens in 129 of the 2,998 R5 rounds (4.3%). Then the bits of 2D + 1 must match: the best of the 2,998 matched 6 bits (out of 10 to 73). Length alone does not decide it either: the target (2D + 1)·2s was longer than m + 1 in rounds 0, 1, 2, 4, 9 and 33 of the first 30,000 (round 33 read 515 bits of an X of about 1,560), so the two lengths cross; after that m + 1 was always longer. In 20,000 rounds (L up to 3.9 million) the low s bits matched in 887 of 19,998 R5 rounds, and the longest agreement was at round 6634, where all 5 bits of 2D+1 matched, but m+1 there is millions of bits longer than the target; in 30,000 rounds the target was longer than m+1 only in the same six early rounds. A proof of non-halting needs a reason why the unread top of X can never equal what the round built from its bottom; none is known.
claims.where: holdouts/1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_0RB---/py/r5_match.py (exact integers, the model step of SOC23Model.v in the deficit form)

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Coq proves the question equivalent to one equation in the model orbit from (2, 5): the machine halts exactly when, at some rule R5 (the end of a second-overflow cascade), the unread rest m of the right counter satisfies m + 1 = (2D + 1)·2s (halts_iff_r5_match). In 400,000 rounds X stayed at least 0.47·L bits away from a corner, and in 3,000 rounds no R5 matched more than 6 bits of 2D + 1 past the first s. No invariant ruling the equation out is known.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine counts one binary number down and another one up, again and again, in phases that get longer and longer. This page shows the real machine in your browser, explains the two counters, and says exactly where a halt could come from.

facts.text: Proved in Lean, including the only way a pass can halt.
A closed model of the whole run: it halts if and only if one rule (R5) meets one equation, which makes a corner X = 2<sup>L</sup>.
No halt in a validated accelerated run (53 jumps).

sections.heading: Four machines, one engine
html: Four holdouts share the first four states of this machine, 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB, and differ only in the last two: 1a 1RB0RF_0RB---, 1b 1RB0RF_1RC---, 1c 1RF0LE_1RA---, 1d 1RF1RC_1RA---. States A to D do almost all of the work; E and F only decide what happens when the head runs into the right part of the tape. This page is about machine 1b; the other three work the same way with different constants.

In 1a and 1b the gaps on the right have lengths 2, 5, 8, 11, ... (3d + 2); in 1c and 1d they have lengths 4, 9, 14, ... (5d + 4). 1a and 1b even agree step for step as long as F only ever reads a 0 followed by another 0, which is what happens in every run we made.

sections.heading: Blocks on the left, gaps on the right
html: Stop the simulator at a moment when the head is in state A on a 0 with a block of 1s to its right. The tape then looks like

Left of the head: blocks of an odd number of 1s separated by single 0s (and one even block at the far left). Right of the head: single 1s separated by gaps whose lengths are 2, 5, 8, .... The odd blocks and the gaps are the digits of two numbers.

sections.heading: How a block of 1s is used up
html: From such a moment to the next (a pass) the head eats the block 1^m two cells at a time: states A, B and C carry one 1 at a time to the left part, then D runs right and writes into the first gap. What happens depends on m:

• m even: two 1s move to the left, the first gap gets one cell shorter;
  • m odd: D runs right over all the gaps of the smallest size, (0^2 1); those gaps merge into one long gap, and the first larger gap is cut;
  • m = 2 or 3: the block merges with the blocks on its left and the head walks back to the 0 left of them.
These pass rules are proved in Lean for every value of the block lengths and every surrounding tape (lean/Rules.lean).

sections.heading: One number counts down, another counts up
html: Read the tape at the start of a pass as two binary numbers. Left of the head, going outward, every pair of cells is one bit of E, lowest bit first: 1 1 is a 0 and 1 0 is a 1, down to an even block, the floor. Right of the head, after the top block, every group of 3 cells is one bit of N: 0^3 is a 0 and 0^2 1 is a 1. (So an odd block 1^(2v+1) is v zero bits and a one bit, and a gap is a run of zero bits closed by a one bit.)

With top block 1^3 (mode 3) one pair of passes subtracts 1 from E and adds 1 to N; with 1^5 (mode 5) two pairs subtract 1 from E and add 2 to N. A pair costs a constant plus 4 steps per trailing zero of E plus 6 per trailing one of N, exactly the work of borrowing and carrying.
This is now proved in Lean for every E and N (lean/Counter.lean: run3, run5), and Lean also proves that the run from blank tape reaches this counter after 160 steps (lean/Init.lean).

sections.heading: When the countdown ends
html: When E reaches 0 the floor 1^(2s) is popped into the top block; the next pass pushes s single 1s, which is E ≈ 2s − 1, all ones, and the mode switches between 3 and 5. N is left on the right, but the pass that cut it leaves a gap of the wrong size, a defect, in front of it.

Defects are worked off in a cascade of short sub-phases: a gap one cell too long collapses into a block 1^2; a block 1^2 followed by a gap makes the next gap one too short; a gap one too short followed by a single 1 is cut and hands its defect to the next gap. Sometimes N is swallowed into the left part entirely and restarts at 0. Then a clean countdown runs again. Since the floor gains 2 cells each time E passes a power of two, the floor is about twice the bit length of the largest E so far, and phases grow fast.

The accelerator py/jump2.py simulates the cascades directly and jumps over every clean countdown with the Lean-proved rule. In about 15 minutes on one core it made 107 jumps and reached step 2.53·10819 with no halt (the run was stopped there, not by a failure).

sections.heading: How it could stop
html: The machine halts only when F reads a 1. From a pass start that happens exactly when an odd pass, after the gaps of the smallest size, meets a gap of length one followed by a block of two or more 1s (pass_odd_halt, proved). In the language above that needs two defects at once: a gap cut down to length one, directly in front of the 1^2 left by another defect. In every transition seen so far a single defect was worked off without harm.

During a countdown there are no defects at all, so a halt can only come inside a transition cascade. In the 6.3 million passes that the round-2 run of 1b simulated directly (between its 107 jumps), the right part never held more than one defect, never more than one 1^2 block, and the fatal precursor (a gap one cell short directly followed by a block of two or more) never occurred.

sections.heading: A closed model: it halts exactly at a corner
html: Coq proves a second, closed description of the same counters, which also covers the transitions. A round starts at cfgL L 0 X: a left counter of L digits (10 or 11) at zero, and a right counter X (digits 100 and 000). The left counter is worked off against the right one; when it overflows, the low block of X is stripped into one of two shifted right counters, and one of five rebuild rules starts the next countdown. Eight raw rules, each proved for every parameter by symbolic execution, cover everything, for 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_0RB--- and 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_1RC--- alike.

The model step is a computable function with an invariant, and it has exactly one dead end: the corner X = 2L, a full right counter. So a halt needs the orbit from (2, 5), where both machines arrive from blank tape, to reach a corner (halts_needs_corner). Coq also proves the converse: from a corner the machine always halts, for every L (corner_halts). The left counter is counted down against a right counter that is twice too large, overflows a second time and gains a digit, the right part becomes a short counter with the end marker 0011, it is counted up twice, and a final sweep reads a 1 in state F. So the machine halts if and only if the orbit hits a corner (halts_iff_corner); directly simulated, the corner tape halts in 2L+5 − 3L − 18 steps.
The last rounds: L and how many bits separate X from the corner 2L.

What is open is whether the orbit ever hits a corner. A round reads X from its low end and, apart from two early rounds that read all of it, stops at rule R5 with a top part m of X unread. Counting the left counter by how far it is below full, D, the next X is 2L' + m + 1 − (2D+1)·2s, so a corner needs m + 1 = (2D+1)·2s: the unread top of X must equal a number built from the bits the round read. That number has about 2.5 times as many bits as the part read, so the round would have to read about 29% of X and the remaining 71% would have to match exactly. In 400,000 rounds (L up to 132 million) only round 10 read that much, no round from round 35 on read more than 22.3%, X stayed at least 0.47·L bits from 2L, and nothing proved prevents a hit.

sections.heading: The cascade has one door
html: A round of the model has two halves. First the left counter is counted down against the right counter X until it overflows. Then comes the cascade: the right counter is read from its low end, block by block, by a chain of second overflows (rules R1 to R5). The cascade decides everything. Once it hands over to the plain counter, the rest of the round is a fixed countdown whose end is known in advance.

The cascade reads X as runs 0^h 1 and only looks at whether each h is even or odd. That makes it a reader with four states, S0 or S1 times even or odd h. In S0, an even run moves to S1 and an odd run stays in S0. In S1 with h even, a 0 next starts another run, and a 1 next swallows a whole block 1^j 0 and moves to S0. In S1 with h odd the round stops: that is rule R5, and the part m of X not yet read stays on the tape. Along the way the left counter grows. Write D for how far it is below full. Each block read adds to D, and each overflow that appends s digits turns D into (2D + 1)·2s.

Coq now proves that this cascade has exactly one way to make a corner (SOC23Match.v, halts_iff_r5_match). If X runs out first (R1, R2, R3 with nothing left to read), the next countdown starts from an odd number times a power of two, and that is never a power of two minus one. So it cannot end at a corner. Only R5 can, and only when the unread part satisfies m + 1 = (2D + 1)·2s. The top of X, which earlier rounds left behind, would have to spell exactly the number the round has just built from the bottom of X. The same lemma is checked in Lean for the model (lean/Cascade.lean). So each of the two machines halts if and only if one R5 round meets this equation.

The panel below runs the model and checks every R5 against the equation. The low s bits are the easy part: m must end in exactly s ones. About one R5 in 23 gets that far. After that the bits of 2D + 1 have to match too, and in the first 3,000 rounds the best was 6 of them. Size does not rule a match out either. In six early rounds (the last is round 33) the target was longer than m + 1, and later it is always shorter, so the two lengths cross. A proof that the machine never halts needs a reason why this equation never holds, and none is known.
The last R5 rounds that got past the low s bits, and how far into 2D + 1 they matched.
rows.push("round "+t+": s = "+r.s+", low s bits match, then "+k+" of "+(r.tb-r.s)+" bits of 2D+1; m+1 has "+r.mb+" bits");}

sections.heading: What is missing
html: The counter is proved; the transitions are not. A transition is a cascade whose course depends on the low bits of E and N and on where earlier defects sit, and no closed formula for the configuration after it is known, in the language of passes. The Coq model above sidesteps this: it describes whole rounds as one explicit map, so the question is now about that map alone. What is missing is an invariant of the map that rules out the one halting equation, m + 1 = (2D + 1)·2s at rule R5.
Because the phases grow so fast, simulation can only ever check a few dozen transitions; whatever decides this machine has to be an argument about all transitions at once.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.036).
After 109 steps the tape spans 137 cells (6 left of the start, 127 right), with a density of 1s of 0.46.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Almost the same run as 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_0RB--- (observed, not proved). Tape and head are the same at all but 12 of the first 107 steps from blank tape. The two runs part 6 times, each time for a step or two and by one cell, first at step 9 and last at step 4,072,133, and come together again. The tables differ and are not renamings of each other. While the runs agree, the states pair up as A–A, B–B, C–C, D–D, E–E, F–F (this machine first).

summary: Family 1b: two binary counters, E written in odd blocks left of the head counting down and N written in gaps right of it counting up (proved in Lean for every size); when E runs out the floor block becomes a new E and defects appear on the right; it halts only if two defects meet. No halt to 2.53·10^819 steps (accelerated run). Coq: a closed model shared with its twin; it halts if and only if the model orbit hits a corner X = 2^L, avoided for 400,000 rounds. Open.
